questions.question: What is the difference between EDA and CDA?
questions.reference_answer: EDA explores the data to understand trends and patterns without formal hypothesis testing and is open-ended; CDA tests a clear hypothesis against the data, often with statistical tests. EDA comes before CDA and informs its hypotheses.
key_points: EDA: open-ended exploration, no formal hypothesis testing
CDA: tests clear hypotheses with statistical tests

questions.question: What is the purpose of EDA?
questions.reference_answer: To understand the data's structure and extract key variables, gain insights by uncovering patterns and anomalies, detect outliers and validate assumptions, and lay the groundwork for later analyses.

questions.question: What is the difference between nominal and ordinal scales?
questions.reference_answer: Nominal scales are categories without an inherent order (e.g. shirt colours); ordinal scales have a clear order but are not measured on a standard scale (e.g. T-shirt sizes, agreement ratings).
key_points: ordinal: clear order, no standard scale
examples: colours vs sizes / survey responses

questions.question: What does the empirical rule (68-95-99.7) say?
questions.reference_answer: For a normal distribution about 68% of the data lies within one SD of the mean, about 95% within two SDs and about 99.7% within three SDs.

questions.question: What are the rules of thumb for interpreting a skewness value?
questions.reference_answer: Below -1 or above 1: highly skewed; between -1 and -0.5 or between 0.5 and 1: moderately skewed; between -0.5 and 0.5: approximately symmetric.

questions.question: What is a Q-Q plot and how do you read it?
questions.reference_answer: It compares the quantiles of your data with those of a theoretical (normal) distribution; points on the straight line suggest normality, deviations show departures such as skewness or kurtosis.
key_points: compares data quantiles with theoretical quantiles
points on the line suggest normality

questions.question: For the sample [2, 3, 5, 7, 11], what are the mean and the sample variance?
questions.reference_answer: Mean = 28/5 = 5.6. Squared deviations: 12.96, 6.76, 0.36, 1.96, 29.16, summing to 51.2; sample variance = 51.2/(5 - 1) = 12.8.

questions.question: With mean 50, is a score of 55 unusual if the SD is 10? What if the SD is 1?
questions.reference_answer: z = (55 - 50)/10 = 0.5 SD from the mean (not much); with SD = 1, z = 5 SDs from the mean (a lot, possibly an outlier).

questions.question: When should I divide by n and when by n - 1 when computing a variance?
questions.reference_answer: Divide by n when the data set is the entire population; divide by n - 1 (the degrees of freedom) when it is a sample.
key_points: n - 1 is the degrees of freedom

questions.question: My data have a long tail to the right. How can I make them closer to normal?
questions.reference_answer: A long right tail is positive skew; reduce it with a square-root or log transformation (negative skew is reduced by squaring).

questions.question: Why do statisticians care so much whether a variable looks like a bell curve?
questions.reference_answer: Normality is the most common assumption of statistical tests; if distributions are not approximately normal the test assumptions are violated, so each variable's distribution must be checked and adjusted. The central limit theorem explains why sample means tend to be normal.
key_points: normal distribution is the most common assumption of tests

questions.question: Why does the average of many random samples follow a bell curve even if the population does not?
questions.reference_answer: The central limit theorem: for sufficiently large random samples taken with replacement from a population with mean mu and SD sigma, the distribution of the sample means is approximately normal, regardless of the population's distribution.
key_points: sufficiently large random samples with replacement

questions.question: What does it mean when a distribution has a taller, sharper peak than the normal curve?
questions.reference_answer: It is leptokurtic (higher kurtosis): more data around the mean. A flatter peak is platykurtic; the normal distribution is mesokurtic with kurtosis 0.

questions.question: According to the four levels of measurement table, which level is the only one with a true zero, and which properties does an interval scale have?
questions.reference_answer: Only the ratio scale has a true or meaningful zero. An interval scale categorizes and labels, ranks categories in order and has known, equal intervals, but no true zero.
key_points: only ratio has a true zero

questions.question: Which display does the lecture recommend for each combination of categorical and continuous variables?
questions.reference_answer: Categorical + categorical: crosstabs; categorical + continuous: box plots and bar plots; continuous + continuous: scatter plots.

questions.question: In the stem-and-leaf plots, what are the median and quartiles of the 'during' data?
and how do you decide which points are outliers?

history.content: What does the box in a boxplot show?
The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile (the interquartile range), and the line inside it is the median.

questions.reference_answer: A point is an outlier if it lies more than 1.5 times the IQR beyond the box: below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR. Outliers are plotted individually beyond the whiskers.
key_points: below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR

questions.question: is it still useful when there are many variables?

history.content: How do I look at the relationship between two continuous variables?
Use a scatter plot of one variable against the other.

questions.reference_answer: For more than two variables you can use pairwise scatterplots (a scatterplot matrix), which can be somewhat ineffective for categorical data, or parallel coordinates, where alpha blending helps with many lines.

questions.question: What is univariate data, and which plots are used to display it?
questions.reference_answer: Univariate data are observations on a single variable; they can be displayed with histograms, stem-and-leaf plots, boxplots and Q-Q plots.
